hook.text: Banks pay you 0.5% on your savings. They charge borrowers 7%. That 6.5% gap is where the profit lives.

buildup.text: The net interest margin is the difference between what a bank earns on loans and what it pays on deposits.

discovery.text: A typical bank makes 2-3% NIM. On $100 billion in assets, that's $2-3 billion in annual revenue from the spread alone.

twist.text: When interest rates drop near zero, the spread shrinks.

climax.text: The interest spread is banking's oldest trick. Borrow cheap, lend expensive, keep the difference.

punchline.text: Pay low, charge high. The interest spread is banking's core engine.

quiz.question: What is net interest margin?
options: The gap between loan income and deposit costs

topics.title: Why Savings Rates Are So Low

hook.text: Your savings account earns almost nothing. The bank lends your money at 7% and keeps most of the profit.

buildup.text: Banks set deposit rates based on competition. If most banks pay 0.5%, the market finds that acceptable.

discovery.text: Banks don't need to attract deposits aggressively. They have more deposits than loan demand in most periods.

twist.text: Online banks pay 4-5% because they have no branches. Your local bank spends that margin on real estate and tellers.

climax.text: Low savings rates aren't greed. They're the cost of branches, ATMs, and local presence passed on to depositors.

punchline.text: Your low rate funds the branch. Online banks skip branches and pay you more.

quiz.question: Why do online banks offer higher savings rates?
options: They have no branch costs to cover

hook.text: When the Fed raises rates, bank profits usually jump. They raise loan rates faster than they raise deposit rates.

buildup.text: A 1% rate hike might add 1% to mortgage rates immediately. But your savings account rate climbs by just 0.25%.

discovery.text: This lag is called deposit beta. Banks deliberately delay passing rate increases to savers to widen their spread.

twist.text: When rates fall, the opposite happens. Banks drop loan rates slowly and slash deposit rates immediately.

climax.text: Banks always adjust rates in their favor. Rising or falling, the timing benefits the bank, not the depositor.

punchline.text: Rates up: your savings lag. Rates down: your savings fall first.

quiz.question: What is 'deposit beta'?
options: The delay in passing rate increases to depositors

hook.text: Banks lend money for 30 years but take deposits that can leave tomorrow. This mismatch is called duration risk.

buildup.text: A bank issues a 30-year mortgage at 4%. If rates rise to 6%, that mortgage is now worth less than its face value.

discovery.text: Duration risk means banks hold assets that lose value when rates change. The longer the loan, the bigger the risk.

twist.text: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed because of duration risk. They held long-term bonds that lost $15 billion when rates rose.

climax.text: Lending long and borrowing short is how banks profit. It's also how they die when interest rates move against them.

punchline.text: Lend for 30 years, fund it daily. Duration risk is banking's core danger.

quiz.question: What is duration risk?
options: The mismatch between long-term loans and short-term deposits

hook.text: Checking accounts pay zero interest. Banks lend that money at 7%. Free deposits are the most profitable funding source.

buildup.text: Banks call non-interest-bearing deposits 'core deposits.' They're stable, free.

discovery.text: JPMorgan has $2.4 trillion in deposits. A large share paying zero interest generates billions in free lending capital.

twist.text: Banks spend heavily on free checking perks to attract these deposits.

climax.text: Free checking isn't charity. It's the cheapest funding a bank can get, and they would spend a lot to keep it.

punchline.text: Free checking pays the bank, not you. Zero-interest deposits are pure profit.

quiz.question: Why do banks offer free checking accounts?
options: Zero-interest deposits are the cheapest source of lending capital

hook.text: US banks collected $30 billion in overdraft fees in a single year. A $5 coffee that overdraws costs you $35.

buildup.text: Overdraft protection sounds helpful. But it charges $35 each time you spend more than your balance, sometimes daily.

discovery.text: Banks reorder transactions to maximize overdraft fees.

twist.text: 80% of overdraft fees are paid by 9% of customers, usually the poorest account holders living paycheck to paycheck.

climax.text: Overdraft fees are a regressive tax on poverty. The less money you have, the more the bank charges you.

punchline.text: $30 billion from overdrafts. The poorest customers pay the most.

quiz.question: Who pays the most overdraft fees?
options: About 9% of customers, usually the poorest

hook.text: Using an out-of-network ATM costs $3 from the ATM owner plus $2.50 from your bank.

buildup.text: The ATM itself costs about $0.50 per transaction to operate. The rest is pure profit split between two banks.

discovery.text: US banks earn over $7 billion in ATM fees annually. It's a small revenue stream per transaction but massive at scale.

twist.text: Neobanks reimburse ATM fees to attract customers. They lose a few dollars per user but gain deposits worth thousands.

climax.text: ATM fees exist because convenience has a price. Banks charge not for the service, but for the urgency.

punchline.text: $5.50 to get your own cash. ATM fees profit from your urgency.

quiz.question: How much do US banks earn from ATM fees annually?

hook.text: Sending a domestic wire transfer costs $25-30. The actual processing cost to the bank is under $1.

buildup.text: Wire transfers move through the Fedwire system. The Federal Reserve charges banks $0.25 per wire.

discovery.text: International wires cost $40-50 and pass through correspondent banks. Each one takes a cut, adding layers of fees.

twist.text: Fintech apps like Wise charge 0.5-1% for international transfers. Banks charge 3-5% hidden in the exchange rate.

climax.text: Wire fees are legacy pricing. The cost is low, the markup is high, and only competition from fintech is changing it.

punchline.text: Costs the bank under $1. Costs you $25. Wire fees are pure markup.

quiz.question: What does the Federal Reserve charge banks per wire transfer?

hook.text: Some banks charge $12-15 per month just to keep your account open. That's $180 per year for the privilege of a balance.

buildup.text: Maintenance fees are waived if you maintain a minimum balance, usually $1,500-$5,000. Poorer customers can't qualify.

discovery.text: Banks profit twice: earn interest on the required minimum balance and collect fees from anyone who can't maintain it.

twist.text: Online banks eliminated maintenance fees. The fee survives only because traditional banks have branches to fund.

climax.text: Maintenance fees punish small balances. The less money you have, the more banking costs you.

punchline.text: $180 per year to hold your money. Minimum balance rules favor the wealthy.

quiz.question: How can maintenance fees typically be avoided?

hook.text: Swipe your card abroad and your bank charges 3% on every purchase. A $100 dinner costs you $103 before tip.

buildup.text: The foreign transaction fee covers currency conversion. Visa charges 1%. Your bank adds another 2% as profit.

discovery.text: Banks earn billions from foreign transactions. The 3% fee applies to every purchase, from hotels to coffee.

twist.text: Premium credit cards waive foreign fees. But they charge $95-550 in annual fees — you pay up front instead.

climax.text: Foreign transaction fees convert travel into revenue. Every tourist is a profit center for their bank back home.

punchline.text: 3% on every swipe abroad. Your vacation funds your bank's profits.

quiz.question: What is a typical foreign transaction fee?

hook.text: US banks hold $12 trillion in mortgage debt. A 30-year mortgage at 7% pays the bank more in interest than the home.

buildup.text: A $400,000 mortgage at 7% over 30 years costs $558,000 in interest alone. The borrower pays nearly $1 million total.

discovery.text: Banks also charge origination fees of 0.5-1%. On a $400,000 loan, that's $2,000-$4,000 before a single payment is made.

twist.text: Banks often sell mortgages to investors and keep the servicing fee. They profit without holding the risk.

climax.text: Mortgages are the ultimate banking product. Long duration, secured by real property, and profitable at every stage.

punchline.text: $558,000 in interest on a $400,000 loan. Mortgages are profit machines.

quiz.question: How much interest does a $400,000 mortgage at 7% generate over 30 years?

hook.text: The average credit card interest rate is 24%. That makes credit cards the most profitable lending product in banking.

buildup.text: Americans carry $1.1 trillion in credit card debt. At 24% interest, that generates over $260 billion in annual interest.

discovery.text: Banks fund credit card loans with deposits at 0.5%. The spread between 0.5% and 24% is enormous profit per dollar lent.

twist.text: Only half of cardholders carry a balance. The other half use cards for free and earn rewards.

climax.text: Credit cards are the most profitable bank product because the interest rate is high and customers rarely question it.

punchline.text: 24% interest on $1.1 trillion in debt. Credit cards are banking's gold mine.

quiz.question: What is the average credit card interest rate in the US?

hook.text: Car dealerships mark up your auto loan rate by 1-2% and keep the difference. The bank and dealer both profit from you.

buildup.text: The bank offers the dealer a rate of 5%. The dealer tells you the rate is 7%. That 2% markup is the dealer's commission.

discovery.text: US auto loan debt is $1.6 trillion. Banks earn interest while dealers earn markups. The borrower pays both.

twist.text: Getting pre-approved before visiting the dealer eliminates the markup. Most buyers don't know this simple trick.

climax.text: Auto lending shows how banking profits are shared with distribution partners. The dealer sells access to your wallet.

punchline.text: Dealer marks up your rate by 2%. Pre-approval saves you thousands.

quiz.question: How do car dealerships profit from auto loans?
options: They mark up the bank's rate and keep the difference

hook.text: Small business loans charge 6-13% interest plus origination fees of 1-5%. A $100,000 loan costs $5,000 just to open.

buildup.text: Banks consider small businesses risky. Higher rates and fees compensate for the chance the business fails.

discovery.text: SBA-guaranteed loans reduce bank risk. The government covers 75-85% of losses, yet banks still charge full rates.

twist.text: Big banks approve only 13% of small business loan requests. Community banks approve 49%.

climax.text: Small business lending is high-margin, high-risk. Banks profit from fees and rates that reflect risk they've often.

punchline.text: High rates plus fees plus government guarantees. Banks profit while risk shifts.

quiz.question: What approval rate do big banks have for small business loans?

hook.text: US student loan debt is $1.7 trillion. Banks and loan servicers earn billions managing payments on degrees already.

buildup.text: Loan servicers collect payments, manage accounts, and process forgiveness applications.

discovery.text: Private student loans charge 4-14% interest. Unlike mortgages, student debt cannot be discharged in bankruptcy.

twist.text: Government-backed student loans are risk-free for servicers.

climax.text: Student loan servicing is banking's safest revenue. Guaranteed income, no risk, and a borrower who can't walk away.

punchline.text: $1.7 trillion in debt you can't escape. Student loans are risk-free for banks.

quiz.question: What makes student loan debt unique?
options: It generally cannot be discharged in bankruptcy

hook.text: Goldman Sachs earned $7.5 billion from trading in 2023.

buildup.text: Proprietary trading means banks bet their own money on market movements.

discovery.text: Banks have informational advantages. They see order flow, market data, and client positions.

twist.text: The Volcker Rule restricts prop trading. But banks reclassify trades as 'market making' to continue trading with client.

climax.text: Trading desks generate huge profits but also create the risk that blows up banks.

punchline.text: Billions from trading. Profits are private. Losses get bailouts.

quiz.question: What is proprietary trading?
options: Banks trading their own capital for profit

hook.text: Banks quote buy and sell prices for securities. They buy at $99.95 and sell at $100.05. That $0.10 spread is profit.

buildup.text: Market makers provide liquidity. They stand ready to buy or sell at any time, keeping markets functional.

discovery.text: On billions of daily trades, the spread adds up to enormous revenue.

twist.text: Electronic trading has compressed spreads. What was $0.10 is now $0.01. Banks make up for it with massive volume.

climax.text: Market making earns a tiny amount per trade on a massive number of trades. Scale is what makes it profitable.

punchline.text: Pennies per trade, billions in total. Market making profits from volume.

quiz.question: How do market makers profit?
options: By the bid-ask spread on each trade

hook.text: The forex market trades $7.5 trillion daily. Banks handle most of it and profit from every currency conversion.

buildup.text: Corporations need to convert currencies for international trade. Banks charge a spread on every conversion.

discovery.text: Five banks control 50% of global forex trading. Citibank, JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, UBS.

twist.text: In 2013, banks were caught rigging forex rates. Traders coordinated in chat rooms called 'The Cartel' and 'The Mafia.'

climax.text: Forex is hugely profitable because every international transaction needs a currency conversion.

punchline.text: $7.5 trillion daily. Five banks control half of all currency trades.

quiz.question: How much is traded daily in the global forex market?

hook.text: The global derivatives market is worth $632 trillion in notional value.

buildup.text: Derivatives are contracts whose value depends on something else: interest rates, currencies, stocks, or commodities.

discovery.text: Banks earn fees structuring custom derivatives for clients. A single interest rate swap can generate millions in fees.

twist.text: In 2008, AIG sold $440 billion in credit default swaps it couldn't pay.

climax.text: Derivatives are insurance contracts that generate fees for banks.

punchline.text: $632 trillion market. Huge fees. But 2008 showed the hidden danger.

quiz.question: What is the notional value of the global derivatives market?

hook.text: When a company goes public, investment banks charge 3-7% of the total raised.

buildup.text: Underwriting means the bank buys all the shares first, then resells them to investors. The bank guarantees the sale.

discovery.text: Banks also underwrite bond issuances. Governments and corporations pay fees to have banks distribute their debt.

twist.text: Banks sometimes underprice IPOs deliberately. The 'pop' on day one makes their clients happy and brings more deal flow.

climax.text: Underwriting is risk for hire. Banks get paid to absorb the uncertainty of selling new securities to the market.

punchline.text: Up to 7% of billions raised. IPO underwriting is high-stakes fee income.

quiz.question: What percentage do banks typically charge for underwriting an IPO?

hook.text: Every time you swipe a card, the merchant pays 1.5-3% to the bank. US interchange fees exceeded $100 billion in 2022.

buildup.text: The fee is split between the card network, the issuing bank, and the payment processor. The bank gets the largest share.

discovery.text: Interchange fees fund credit card rewards. Banks earn 2% on your purchase and give you back 1% in points.

twist.text: Merchants raise prices to cover interchange fees. Cash customers subsidize card users' rewards without knowing it.

climax.text: Interchange fees are invisible to cardholders but visible in every price tag. You pay whether you use a card or not.

punchline.text: $100 billion in swipe fees. Hidden in every purchase you make.

quiz.question: Who ultimately pays interchange fees?
options: Merchants, who pass the cost to all customers through higher prices

hook.text: Banks charge wealthy clients 1% annually to manage their money.

buildup.text: Wealth management includes investment advice, tax planning, and estate planning.

discovery.text: Morgan Stanley's wealth division manages $5 trillion. At roughly 1% in fees, that's $50 billion in annual revenue.

twist.text: Studies show most managed portfolios underperform index funds.

climax.text: Wealth management sells confidence, not performance. Banks profit from the comfort of having an expert.

punchline.text: 1% fee on trillions. Wealth management sells comfort, not results.

quiz.question: How do most managed portfolios perform compared to index funds?

hook.text: Your bank knows every purchase you make. That spending data is valuable to advertisers, retailers, and data brokers.

buildup.text: Banks anonymize and aggregate transaction data. They sell spending trends to hedge funds, retailers.

discovery.text: A hedge fund can predict a company's quarterly revenue by analyzing credit card spending data.

twist.text: Banks claim data is anonymized. But with enough data points, individuals can often be re-identified from spending.

climax.text: Your transaction history is a product. You are the source, advertisers are the buyers, and the bank is the broker.

punchline.text: Banks sell your spending data. You're the product, not just the customer.

quiz.question: Who buys anonymized bank transaction data?
options: Hedge funds, retailers, and marketing firms

hook.text: Miss a credit card payment and you get a $40 late fee plus your interest rate jumps to 29%. One mistake costs hundreds.

buildup.text: US banks collect over $14 billion annually in credit card late fees alone.

discovery.text: Penalty APRs are triggered by a single late payment. Your rate stays elevated for months, costing far more than the fee.

twist.text: The CFPB capped credit card late fees at $8 in 2024. Banks immediately sued to block the rule, protecting $14 billion.

climax.text: Late fees are designed to punish mistakes, but they generate predictable revenue banks depend on and fight to keep.

punchline.text: $14 billion in late fees. Banks sued to keep charging them.

quiz.question: What happens to your interest rate after a missed credit card payment?
options: It can jump to a penalty rate of 29% or higher

hook.text: Banks sell insurance, investments, and credit monitoring alongside checking accounts.

buildup.text: Wells Fargo's strategy was '8 products per household.' Push every customer toward credit cards, mortgages.

discovery.text: Cross-selling works because trust transfers. If you trust a bank with your savings.

twist.text: Wells Fargo opened 3.5 million fake accounts to meet cross-selling targets.

climax.text: Cross-selling is profitable when ethical. But aggressive targets turn bankers into salespeople, customers into quotas.

punchline.text: 8 products per customer. Wells Fargo faked 3.5 million accounts to meet it.

quiz.question: What did Wells Fargo do to meet cross-selling targets?

hook.text: JPMorgan earned $49 billion in profit in 2023. That's more than most countries' GDP. Banking is insanely profitable.

buildup.text: Banks combine interest income, fee income, trading revenue, and wealth management.

discovery.text: Leverage amplifies returns. Banks hold $10 in assets for every $1 in capital.

twist.text: Bank profits are partly subsidized by taxpayers. Deposit insurance, central bank lending.

climax.text: Banking is profitable because it's leveraged, diversified, and backstopped by government.

punchline.text: $49 billion in one year. Leveraged, diversified, and government-backed.

quiz.question: How much profit did JPMorgan earn in 2023?

topics.title: The Cost of Being a Bank

hook.text: Running a bank is expensive. JPMorgan spends $87 billion annually on salaries, technology, branches, and compliance.

buildup.text: Technology alone costs major banks $10-14 billion per year.

discovery.text: Compliance and regulation cost US banks $70 billion annually.

twist.text: Branch costs are declining. Each bank branch costs $2-4 million to operate annually, and customers visit less each year.

climax.text: Banks are technology and compliance companies that happen to take deposits.

punchline.text: $87 billion in annual costs. Banks are tech and compliance companies disguised.

quiz.question: How many technologists does JPMorgan employ?

hook.text: Banks hold $10-12 in assets for every $1 of their own money.

buildup.text: A 1% return on $1 trillion in assets equals $10 billion.

discovery.text: Leverage is why banking seems so profitable. Small margins on borrowed money create big returns for shareholders.

twist.text: Leverage also means a 10% loss in asset values wipes out all equity.

climax.text: Leverage makes banking the world's most rewarding and most dangerous business.

punchline.text: $10 borrowed for every $1 owned. Leverage makes banks rich and fragile.

quiz.question: What does 10:1 leverage mean for a bank?
options: The bank holds $10 in assets for every $1 of its own capital

hook.text: US banks spent $80 billion on stock buybacks in 2022. They used profits to buy back their own shares instead of lending.

buildup.text: Buybacks reduce the number of shares outstanding. Fewer shares means higher earnings per share.

discovery.text: Bank executives are paid in stock. Buybacks directly increase the value of their own compensation packages.

twist.text: Critics argue buyback money should fund more lending or be held as reserves.

climax.text: Buybacks show where bank priorities lie. Profits go to shareholders first, lending second, and communities last.

punchline.text: $80 billion in buybacks. Profits go to shareholders, not to lending.

quiz.question: Why do banks buy back their own stock?
options: To reduce shares outstanding and boost earnings per share

topics.title: The Revolving Door of Banking Profit

hook.text: Banks earned record profits in 2023 while customers faced rising fees, higher loan rates, and low savings yields.

buildup.text: Every product banks sell transfers wealth from customers to shareholders: interest spreads, fees, trading.

discovery.text: The banking profit model is circular: deposits fund loans, loans generate interest.

twist.text: Government guarantees lower the cost of risk. Banks keep the profits in good years and pass losses to taxpayers in bad.

climax.text: Banking's profit engine never stops because it's powered by everyday economic activity.

punchline.text: Every transaction feeds the bank. Banking profits from all economic activity.

quiz.question: What makes banking profits so persistent?
options: Banks profit from essentially all economic activity flowing through them
